mots.sens: This verb means 'to release' or 'to deliver.' In the context of Matthew 26:1, it evokes the idea of bringing an end to a series of discourses, which can symbolize the transition to a crucial moment in Jesus' ministry. Spiritually, this can be perceived as a preparation for the ultimate revelation of His redemptive mission.

This term translates to 'teacher' and emphasizes Jesus' role as a master. It is often used to refer to those who convey spiritual truths. In this verse, it reminds us that Jesus imparted essential teachings to His disciples, preparing them to understand the significance of His impending passion.

This word means 'disciple' or 'student,' and it designates those who follow a teacher to learn. In the context of this verse, it highlights the intimate relationship between Jesus and His disciples, who are called to put His teachings into practice. This underscores the call to discipleship, which involves personal transformation and a commitment to the revealed truth.

1.epoque: This passage is set in the first century, during a time when Judaism was experiencing significant religious and political fervor, with increasing tensions between Jewish and Roman authorities.
1.passage: Matthew 26 marks the beginning of the events leading up to Jesus' crucifixion. After teaching about the kingdom of God and the end times, Jesus announces to His disciples the nearness of His passion.
1.culture: In the Jewish culture of the time, discourses and teachings were crucial for the transmission of faith. Disciples were trained to become teachers in turn, carrying God's word into their communities.
1.interpretation: This verse indicates a significant transition in Jesus' ministry, signaling the end of His public teaching and the beginning of His sacrifice. Spiritually, it reminds us of the importance of listening to and applying Christ's teachings in our daily lives.
1.commentaire: This passage invites us to reflect on the importance of attentively listening to the words of Jesus. As disciples, we are called to put His teachings into practice, especially in times of transition and crisis. It reminds us that every discourse of Christ has a purpose and that we must be ready to follow His example, even when the path seems difficult.

mots.sens: The word 'Πάσχα' (Pascha) refers to the Jewish Passover, a central feast in the Hebrew tradition that commemorates the liberation of the Israelites from slavery in Egypt. Its etymology is linked to the verb 'to pass over,' evoking the transition from death to life. In the Christian context, Passover takes on an additional dimension with the sacrifice of Christ, the true Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world, thus marking a new passage to redemption.

The term 'παραδίδομαι' (paradidomai) means 'to deliver' or 'to betray.' This verb carries connotations of handing over or transferring, often in a context of betrayal. In this verse, it emphasizes the gravity of the act that will be committed against the Son of Man, highlighting Jesus' voluntary sacrifice for humanity while revealing the human nature of betrayal.

The word 'σταυρός' (stauros) means 'cross.' In Roman culture, the cross was a symbol of shame and suffering, but for Christians, it has become the symbol of redemption and God's unconditional love. The crucifixion of Jesus on the cross is the central point of the Christian faith, representing the ultimate sacrifice for the salvation of humanity.

The expression 'Υιός του ανθρώπου' (Huios tou anthropou) translates to 'Son of Man.' Used by Jesus to refer to Himself, it emphasizes His humanity and divine mission. This title echoes the prophecies of Daniel and establishes a link between Christ's humanity and His role as Messiah, thus revealing His divine identity while fully identifying with our human condition.

2.epoque: This passage is set in the historical context of first-century Palestine, under Roman domination, where religious and political tensions were palpable, especially around Jewish festivals.
2.passage: In this chapter, Jesus announces His imminent crucifixion to His disciples, emphasizing the importance of Passover and the profound meaning of His sacrifice. This occurs just before His arrest and trial, marking a decisive turning point in the history of salvation.
2.culture: Passover was a major celebration for the Jews, symbolizing liberation and collective memory. In this context, Jesus reinterprets this feast, linking it to His own sacrifice, which was revolutionary for His disciples.
2.interpretation: This verse announces the nearness of Jesus' crucifixion, highlighting the voluntary nature of His sacrifice for humanity. It invites reflection on the depth of God's love, which allowed His Son to be delivered for our redemption.
2.commentaire: This passage reminds us of the importance of Passover and its fulfillment in Christ. As we meditate on these verses, we are called to recognize the price of our salvation and to live in gratitude for Jesus' sacrifice. It also prompts us to examine our own faithfulness and commitment to the One who gave everything for us.

mots.sens: This term designates the high priest, a central figure in the Jewish religious system. He is responsible for sacrifices and intercession for the people. In the context of this verse, it highlights the religious authority and power of the elites who gather to conspire against Jesus. Spiritually, it sheds light on the struggle between religious authorities and the truth embodied in Christ.

This verb means 'to gather' or 'to assemble.' It evokes the idea of a deliberate gathering for a common purpose, often related to important decisions. In this passage, it underscores the conspiracy orchestrated by the religious leaders against Jesus, indicating a malicious intent. This reminds us of the importance of our motivations during our gatherings, whether spiritual or social.

This term refers to the elders, respected leaders within the Jewish community. They are often associated with wisdom and spiritual authority. Their presence in this verse indicates that the plot against Jesus is not only the work of the priests but also involves the elders, highlighting the depth of corruption within the religious leadership. This challenges us regarding our own integrity as spiritual leaders.

3.epoque: This passage is set in the first century, during the period of Roman domination in Judea, where religious and political tensions were high. The Jewish authorities sought to maintain their power in the face of Jesus' rise and His teachings.
3.passage: In Matthew 26, we enter the last week of Jesus' life, where events accelerate toward His crucifixion. This verse introduces the plot of the religious leaders to arrest Jesus, showing their determination to preserve their authority.
3.culture: The Jewish culture of the time valued the roles of priests and elders, who were seen as guardians of the law and tradition. Their meeting to conspire against Jesus reveals a fracture within the religious community, where tradition is jeopardized by the truth.
3.interpretation: This gathering of the chief priests and elders highlights the resistance of religious authorities to God's revelation in Jesus Christ. Their plot underscores the tension between the light of the Gospel and the darkness of human tradition. Spiritually, it reminds us that truth can often be rejected by those who are attached to their power.
3.commentaire: This verse invites us to reflect on how we respond to the truth of the Gospel. Like the religious leaders, we may be tempted to preserve our comfort or status at the expense of the truth. Let us be vigilant and open to God's work, even when it challenges our traditions or positions.

mots.sens: This term refers to the action of deliberating or planning, involving the construction or establishment of a project. In the context of Matthew 26:4, it highlights the cunning and premeditation of the religious leaders to arrest Jesus. Theologically, this sheds light on the struggle between evil and good, where the religious authorities, who are supposed to represent God, conspire against the Son of God.

This word means 'to cause to die' or 'to take life away.' It carries a connotation of violence and rejection of life. In this verse, it reveals the desire of the religious leaders to eliminate not only Jesus but also the message of the Gospel that he represents, emphasizing the seriousness of sin and the necessity of redemption.

This term means 'cunning' or 'deception.' It evokes the idea of manipulation and trickery, often used by those who seek to divert the truth. Spiritually, this reminds us that evil can disguise itself under appearances of legitimacy, urging believers to remain vigilant against the devil's traps.

4.epoque: This passage is set in the historical context of the 1st century, at a time when tensions between the Jewish religious authorities and Jesus of Nazareth reach their peak. The religious leaders fear losing their power and influence in light of Jesus' teaching.
4.passage: In Matthew 26, we enter the last week of Jesus' life, where events rush toward his crucifixion. This chapter highlights the plots of the religious leaders who seek to eliminate Jesus, revealing their opposition to his ministry.
4.culture: The Jewish culture of the time valued religious authority and tradition, but it was also marked by power struggles. The religious leaders, in seeking to preserve their status, demonstrate how fear and pride can lead to desperate actions.
4.interpretation: This verse illustrates the depth of the opposition Jesus faced, not only from the Romans but also from his own countrymen. Spiritually, this reminds us that even those who claim to serve God can sometimes be in opposition to his purposes.
4.commentaire: This passage teaches us the importance of spiritual vigilance against cunning and deception. As believers, we must be aware of the dangers that threaten our faith and commitment to Christ. It calls us to seek the truth and remain faithful to the Gospel, even when forces oppose us.

mots.sens: This term refers to a feast or religious celebration. In the Jewish context, it refers to major feasts such as Passover, which commemorates Israel's liberation from slavery in Egypt. The spiritual significance of this word underscores the importance of moments of celebration in the believer's life, while highlighting the tensions between religious tradition and the events unfolding in Jesus' life.

This word means tumult or agitation. It evokes a situation of disorder or trouble, often caused by strong emotions or conflicts. In this verse, it underscores the fear of the religious authorities of provoking a violent reaction from the people, revealing their concern for maintaining social order in the face of a perceived threat.

This term refers to the people, often in the context of the people of God. It implies a community united by faith and traditions. In the passage, it highlights the dynamic between the Jewish people and the religious authorities, as well as how the decisions of the leaders can influence the spiritual and social life of the community.

5.epoque: This passage takes place during the time of the Jewish Passover, a crucial moment for the Jewish people, when political and religious tensions were particularly high in Jerusalem under Roman occupation.
5.passage: In Matthew 26, the narrative focuses on the plots of the religious leaders to arrest Jesus, highlighting their fear of a popular uprising. This verse shows their strategy of not acting during the feast to avoid trouble among the people.
5.culture: Passover is a feast of great importance in Jewish culture, marked by rituals and memories of liberation from Egypt. The fear of tumult during this period underscores the sensitivity of the authorities to public opinion and religious fervor.
5.interpretation: This verse reveals the tension between the religious authorities and Jesus' mission. Their desire to avoid tumult shows their lack of understanding of the true nature of the Passover celebration, which should be centered on redemption rather than maintaining order.
5.commentaire: This passage invites us to reflect on how we perceive moments of celebration in our spiritual lives. It reminds us that true liberation and peace come from Christ, even amid turmoil. As believers, we must be careful not to let our human concerns hinder our worship and commitment to God, especially during significant moments.

mots.sens: The term 'Bethany' means 'house of the poor' or 'house of affliction.' This name evokes a place of refuge and comfort, which is significant in the context of Jesus' presence, who brings healing and hope. Spiritually, Bethany represents a space where one can encounter Christ, the healer of souls and bodies.

The word 'leper' refers to a person afflicted with leprosy, a disease considered impure in Jewish culture. In the New Testament, lepers are often symbols of sin and social exclusion. The mention of Simon the leper highlights Jesus' power to restore not only physical health but also dignity and spiritual acceptance.

The term 'house' (οἶκος) refers to a place of living, community, and sharing. In the biblical context, the house is often a symbol of safety and belonging. The house of Simon the leper becomes a space where God's grace is manifested, illustrating that even those who are marginalized can be welcomed into divine communion.

6.epoque: This passage is set in the 1st century, during Jesus' earthly ministry, a period marked by religious and political tensions in Judea under Roman occupation.
6.passage: In this chapter, Jesus prepares for his passion, and this scene in Bethany precedes his arrest. It underscores the importance of spiritual preparation before the crucial events of his life.
6.culture: In the Jewish culture of the time, lepers were often excluded and considered impure. The house of Simon the leper illustrates the possible redemption even for those rejected by society.
6.interpretation: This verse highlights Jesus' closeness to those who suffer and are marginalized. Jesus' presence in the house of Simon the leper symbolizes God's unconditional love and his desire to restore broken lives.
6.commentaire: This passage reminds us that Jesus goes where people need him, even in the most unexpected places. He calls us to be instruments of his grace, to welcome those who are rejected, and to testify to his healing power in our own lives and in the lives of others.

mots.sens: This term refers to something made of alabaster, a precious and translucent stone. In the biblical context, alabaster symbolizes value and beauty, highlighting the importance of the perfume contained in the vase. Spiritually, it evokes the idea that our worship towards God must be precious and authentic, just like this costly perfume.

This word means 'of great value' or 'precious.' It emphasizes the importance and rarity of the perfume, which represents the sacred offering that the woman makes to Jesus. Theologically, it reminds us that our devotion to Christ should be regarded as an invaluable treasure, an act of faith and gratitude towards the One who has given us everything.

Meaning 'to pour out' or 'to shed,' this verb expresses the idea of a deliberate and generous act. In this passage, it symbolizes the total giving of oneself, an act of worship that goes beyond mere religious gestures. Spiritually, it calls us to give ourselves entirely to Christ, offering Him our best without reservation.

7.epoque: This passage is set in the context of the 1st century, at a time when Jesus was nearing the end of His earthly ministry, facing opposition and the imminent betrayal by Judas.
7.passage: In this chapter, Jesus is preparing for His crucifixion, and this act of worship by the woman highlights the recognition of His divinity and His forthcoming sacrifice. It is a moment where faith and devotion are manifested in a tangible way.
7.culture: At that time, anointing with precious perfumes was an act of great value and respect, often reserved for kings or people of high stature. This shows the importance of honor and respect in interpersonal and spiritual relationships.
7.interpretation: This act by the woman is a demonstration of faith and devotion, illustrating that true worship involves personal sacrifice. She recognizes the value of Jesus and offers Him what is most dear to her, an act that is often seen as a foreshadowing of His own sacrifice on the cross.
7.commentaire: This verse teaches us that our worship must be authentic and precious in the eyes of God. Like this woman, we are called to offer our best to Christ, whether through our resources, our time, or our hearts. By recognizing the value of Jesus in our lives, we are encouraged to live an active faith, where each act of worship becomes a reflection of our love for Him.

mots.sens: This term means 'useless' or 'of no value,' and it is often used to express loss or waste. In this context, it underscores the disciples' perception that the anointing of Jesus was an extravagant expense. Spiritually, this reveals a limited understanding of the value of acts of devotion towards Christ, which transcend material considerations.

This word means 'to break' or 'to shatter,' and it is used here to describe the action of breaking the flask of oil. This action symbolizes an act of sacrifice and total devotion towards Jesus. Theologically, it reminds us that our worship should be unreserved, even if it seems extravagant in the eyes of the world.

8.epoque: During Jesus' time, Jewish society was marked by messianic expectations and a strong religious tradition, where acts of devotion were often judged based on their material utility.
8.passage: This verse is set in the context of the last week of Jesus before His crucifixion, where He faces betrayal and distrust, even from His disciples. This moment illustrates the tensions between human understanding and divine revelation.
8.culture: In Jewish culture, anointing was an act of great value and respect, often reserved for special occasions. The disciples, seeing the cost of the oil, reacted according to cultural norms of material value, missing the spiritual depth of the act.
8.interpretation: The disciples' indignation at the anointing of Jesus reveals a struggle between human perception of value and the spiritual reality of worship. This invites us to examine our own priorities and recognize that acts of devotion towards God may seem futile in the eyes of the world, but are of immense value in the kingdom of God.
8.commentaire: This passage teaches us that our worship and sacrifices for Christ should not be measured by material criteria. Like this woman who broke the flask, we are called to give all that we have to honor our Lord. Let us reflect on how we value our time, our resources, and our devotion in our walk with Christ.

mots.sens: This word means 'virgin' and is often used to denote a pure, unblemished person. In the context of this verse, it emphasizes the importance of purity and the spiritual value of actions. It reminds us that some offerings, although considered precious, may be misinterpreted by those who do not understand their true spiritual significance.

This term refers to the poor, those in need, often in a vulnerable situation. In Jewish culture, helping the poor was a moral and spiritual obligation. The word also evokes the idea of dependence and necessity, emphasizing that generosity towards the needy is a fundamental value in the Christian faith.

Meaning 'gold,' this word symbolizes wealth and material value. In this verse, it represents the resources that could be used for charitable works. It reminds us that material goods, while precious, must be placed in the perspective of our spiritual commitment and love for others.

This word means 'necessary' or 'indispensable.' In the context of this verse, it emphasizes that the needs of the poor are a priority that should not be neglected. This challenges us on how we perceive our priorities and resources in the Christian life.

9.epoque: This passage is set in the 1st century, in a Jewish context under Roman domination, where social and economic tensions were palpable.
9.passage: In Matthew 26, we witness the preparation for the passion of Jesus. This verse illustrates the tension between authentic worship and the material concerns of the disciples.
9.culture: Jewish culture valued hospitality and helping the poor, but also criticized excessive spending, making Mary's gesture both magnificent and controversial.
9.interpretation: This verse teaches us that the value of an offering is not measured solely by its material cost, but by the intention of the heart. Jesus highlights the beauty of sincere worship, even if it seems extravagant in the eyes of others.
9.commentaire: This passage invites us to reflect on our priorities and how we use our resources. It reminds us that our worship must be authentic and often may seem out of step with the expectations of the world. By placing God at the center of our actions, we can offer sacrifices that, although perceived as excessive, are in reality profound expressions of our faith and love.

mots.sens: This word means 'good', 'beautiful', or 'noble'. In the context of this verse, it emphasizes the quality of the woman's action who anointed Jesus. The root of this word implies not only an outward beauty but also an inner goodness, suggesting that the woman's act is not only aesthetically pleasing but also morally and spiritually significant. It reminds us that our actions towards God should be marked by sincerity and devotion.

This term means 'to do good' or 'to perform a good deed'. It is derived from 'ἀγαθός' (agathos), which means 'good'. In this verse, Jesus defends the woman's action by calling it good, highlighting the importance of our intentions and actions towards Christ. It teaches us that even our small gestures of devotion can have great spiritual value in the eyes of God.

This word means 'woman' and can also refer to a wife. In the biblical context, it often evokes the dignity and role of women in society. By defending the woman, Jesus shows that He values her act of devotion, regardless of her social status. This underscores the inclusivity of the Gospel message and the importance of each individual in the kingdom of God.

10.epoque: This passage takes place in the 1st century, in the context of Roman-occupied Palestine, where social and religious norms were strict and often patriarchal.
10.passage: In Matthew 26, Jesus is preparing for his crucifixion. This chapter highlights the events leading up to his passion, including the anointing of Jesus by a woman, an act of devotion that is misunderstood by some of his disciples.
10.culture: At that time, women often held a lower status in society. However, the actions of this woman show that faith and devotion transcend cultural and social norms.
10.interpretation: Jesus reminds his disciples that love and devotion towards Him are paramount, and that sincere actions, even if they seem extravagant in the eyes of others, are precious. He defends the woman, emphasizing that her act is a testimony of authentic faith.
10.commentaire: This verse teaches us the importance of recognizing and valuing acts of devotion, even when they are criticized. We are called to act with love and to do good, regardless of others' opinions. By imitating the faith of this woman, we can offer our best to Christ, knowing that every act of devotion counts in His kingdom.

mots.sens: This term refers to the poor, those in material or spiritual need. It comes from the root meaning 'to be reduced to a state of begging'. In this verse, it evokes not only the reality of economic difficulties but also the spiritual condition of humanity, highlighting the importance of compassion and help towards those who suffer.

This word means 'always' or 'at all times'. It emphasizes the constancy and inevitability of the presence of the poor in human society. Spiritually, it reminds us that the needs of others are a permanent reality, calling for a continuous response from believers.

This personal pronoun means 'I' and is used here to emphasize the personal presence of Jesus. In the context of this verse, it highlights the importance of a personal relationship with Christ, which is unique and cannot be replaced by any work or act of charity.

11.epoque: In Jesus' time, society was marked by deep economic inequalities, with a large part of the population living in poverty. Jesus' teachings took place in a context where charity and help for the needy were important values, but often neglected by religious and political elites.
11.passage: This verse is situated in the Passion narrative, where Jesus prepares his disciples for his imminent death. It is spoken in response to a criticism of the use of expensive perfume to honor Jesus, highlighting the value of the relationship with him compared to external works.
11.culture: In the Jewish culture of the time, helping the poor was a religious obligation, but often spiritual concerns were set aside in favor of ritual conformity. Jesus challenges this dynamic by emphasizing that his presence among them is temporary and precious.
11.interpretation: Jesus' teaching reminds us that, although the poor are always present, his physical presence among them is unique and should be honored. This invites us to reflect on our priorities and recognize the value of our relationship with Christ, which transcends the works we can accomplish.
11.commentaire: This verse calls us to balance our commitment to charitable works with our worship and devotion to Christ. It reminds us that while we must help the poor, we should never lose sight of the importance of our personal relationship with Jesus. As believers, we are called to live this tension, serving others while placing Christ at the center of our lives.

mots.sens: This word means 'anointing' or 'perfume'. It is derived from the root 'χρίω' (chrió), which means 'to anoint'. In the context of this verse, it evokes the idea of consecration and preparation for a sacred mission. Spiritually, it underscores the importance of Jesus' anointing, who is both a king and a priest, and foreshadows his ultimate sacrifice.

This term means 'body'. It refers to the physical entity of Jesus, but also to the notion of his body as a sacrifice. In this verse, it highlights the humanity of Christ and the importance of his body in the redemption plan. It reminds us that Jesus' sacrifice is both physical and spiritual, embodying God's love for humanity.

This word means 'tomb' or 'grave'. It is related to the idea of death and resting place. In the context of this verse, it anticipates Jesus' death and burial, highlighting the importance of his sacrifice for the salvation of believers. Theologically, it reminds us that Christ's death is not the end, but the beginning of a new life for those who believe in him.

12.epoque: This passage is set in the context of Judea in the 1st century, a period marked by Roman occupation and religious tensions between the Pharisees, Sadducees, and Jesus' followers.
12.passage: In Matthew 26, we witness the last days of Jesus before his crucifixion. This verse is part of a narrative where a woman anoints Jesus, an act that symbolizes her devotion and preparation for his imminent death.
12.culture: Anointing with perfume was a common cultural practice to honor guests and mark important moments. In the Jewish context, it also had strong religious and symbolic connotations, often associated with royalty and holiness.
12.interpretation: The act of pouring perfume on Jesus' body is an anticipation of his death and burial. It reveals the spiritual understanding of the woman who, unlike the disciples, recognizes the significance of Jesus' mission and his forthcoming sacrifice.
12.commentaire: This verse invites us to reflect on our own devotion to Christ. Like this woman, we are called to recognize the importance of Jesus' sacrifice and to offer him our worship and service. By understanding the depth of his love and sacrifice, we are encouraged to live a life that glorifies God and testifies to our faith.

mots.sens: This word means 'good news' and specifically refers to the message of salvation through Jesus Christ. It is derived from the verb 'euangelizō', which means 'to announce good news'. In the context of this verse, it emphasizes the importance of proclaiming Christ's redemptive work throughout the world, and it also evokes the responsibility of believers to share this news with passion and devotion.

This verb means 'to remember' or 'to commemorate'. It carries the idea of keeping something important in mind, often related to significant actions. In this verse, it highlights the importance of remembering acts of faith and devotion, such as those of the woman who anointed Jesus, reminding us that our actions for Christ can have an eternal impact and be recognized in the history of salvation.

13.epoque: This verse is set in the context of the 1st century, at a time when Jesus was on His way to His crucifixion, a pivotal moment in the history of salvation. Believers faced both religious and political challenges, and Jesus' message was revolutionary for His time.
13.passage: This passage is part of the account of the Passion of Jesus, where He prepares for His death. Matthew chapter 26 describes the events leading up to the crucifixion, including the anointing of Jesus by a woman, which is an act of devotion and recognition of His messiahship.
13.culture: In the Jewish culture of the time, acts of devotion, such as anointing, were of great symbolic value. Honor and respect towards religious figures were essential, and this act by the woman breaks social norms, illustrating a deep love and commitment to Jesus.
13.interpretation: This verse teaches us that acts of faith and devotion, even if they seem insignificant in the eyes of the world, are precious in God's sight. The promise that this woman will always be mentioned in memory of her act shows that God honors those who offer Him authentic and sincere worship.
13.commentaire: This passage calls us to reflect on our own devotion to Christ. Are we willing to make sacrifices for Him, even if it goes against social expectations? By sharing the gospel and honoring acts of faith, we participate in God's work and contribute to the eternal memory of those who have served faithfully.

mots.sens: The name 'Ioudas' means 'Praise the Lord'. It is derived from the Hebrew word 'Yehouda', which has connotations of praise and acknowledgment towards God. In the context of this verse, this name takes on a tragic dimension, as the one who bears this name, Judas Iscariot, becomes the ultimate traitor, betraying the Son of God for money. This reminds us that even those called to be close to Christ can distance themselves from Him through deliberate choices.

This term refers to a council or assembly of people who make decisions. In this passage, it refers to the chief priests who, by their religious authority, seek to arrest Jesus. The notion of council implies planning and intentionality in their actions, thus highlighting the gravity of Judas' betrayal and the conspiracy against Christ.

This verb means 'to lose', 'to destroy', or 'to annihilate'. In the context of Judas' betrayal, it evokes the spiritual loss and destruction that his decision brings, not only for himself but also for those who follow Jesus. It warns us of the disastrous consequences our choices can have on our lives and the lives of others.

This word means 'disciple' or 'student'. It designates those who follow a master to learn from him. In this verse, Judas is identified as one of the twelve disciples, which underscores the closeness he had with Jesus and the importance of faithfulness in our Christian walk. It challenges us regarding our own commitment to Christ.

14.epoque: The passage is set in the 1st century, during the period of Roman domination in Palestine, where religious and political tensions were high between the Jewish authorities and the Roman occupiers.
14.passage: This verse is found in the context of the last week of Jesus before His crucifixion. Judas, one of the twelve disciples, makes the decision to betray his master, marking a tragic turning point in the history of salvation.
14.culture: At this time, betrayal was considered one of the worst crimes, especially in a context where loyalty and honor were fundamental values. Judas, by betraying Jesus, acts against these values, which deeply shocks his contemporaries.
14.interpretation: Judas' act serves as a warning about human nature and the temptation of sin. Even among those called to follow Christ, there can be hearts that turn away for personal gain. This prompts us to examine our own faithfulness to the Lord.
14.commentaire: This verse reminds us that proximity to Christ does not guarantee faithfulness. Judas, despite his status as a disciple, chose to betray his master for selfish reasons. This encourages us to remain vigilant in our walk with God, to constantly seek His heart, and not to let the temptations of the world lead us astray.

mots.sens: This term refers to silver, more specifically silver coins. In the biblical context, it often symbolizes material wealth, but also betrayal and greed. The value of the thirty pieces of silver evokes the price of betrayal, in accordance with the prophecy of Zechariah 11:12-13, thus underscoring the gravity of Judas' choice.

This verb means 'to deliver' or 'to betray'. It implies a deliberate act of handing over or transferring, often in a context of betrayal. In this verse, it highlights Judas' conscious decision to deliver Jesus, which has profound spiritual and theological repercussions, illustrating the struggle between good and evil.

This word means 'slave' or 'servant'. In the New Testament, it is often used to designate those who are fully devoted to a master. In the context of Judas' betrayal, it raises questions about loyalty and service, shedding light on the nature of commitment to Christ.

15.epoque: This passage is set in the historical context of 1st century Palestine, under Roman occupation, where religious and political tensions were high.
15.passage: Matthew 26 describes the final days of Jesus before His crucifixion, highlighting Judas' betrayal and the plots of the religious leaders to arrest Jesus.
15.culture: In Jewish culture, betrayal for money was particularly abhorrent, and delivering an innocent person for a sum of money raises profound moral and ethical questions.
15.interpretation: This verse illustrates the depth of human betrayal in light of Christ's holiness. Judas, in exchange for thirty pieces of silver, chooses material gain at the expense of his relationship with the Messiah, thus symbolizing the temptation that money represents in spiritual life.
15.commentaire: This passage reminds us of the importance of our faithfulness to Christ, even in the face of material temptations. It prompts us to reflect on our own priorities and what we are willing to sacrifice for our faith. As disciples, we must question our commitment and loyalty to the Lord, choosing to follow His ways rather than those of the world.

mots.sens: This verb means 'to deliver', 'to hand over', or 'to abandon'. It evokes the idea of entrusting something to someone else, often with a connotation of betrayal. In the context of Matthew 26:16, it emphasizes the act of Judas who, by his decision, abandons Jesus to his enemies, thus revealing the human heart in the face of temptation and greed. Spiritually, this reminds us of the seriousness of betrayal and the importance of remaining faithful to our commitment to Christ.

This term means 'favorable occasion' or 'opportune moment'. It implies an opportunity that arises to act, often with a nuance of planning or foresight. In this verse, it highlights Judas's determination to seek a propitious moment to betray Jesus, illustrating how evil can be premeditated and how sin can infiltrate our lives. Theologically, this challenges us to be vigilant against the opportunities for sin that present themselves to us.

16.epoque: This passage is set in the first century, in a context where Palestine was under Roman rule, and where religious and political tensions were high between Jewish authorities and the followers of Jesus.
16.passage: Matthew 26 focuses on the events leading up to the crucifixion of Jesus, highlighting the plots against him and the betrayal of Judas, which is a major turning point in the history of salvation.
16.culture: At this time, betrayal was considered one of the most infamous acts, and Judas's role in betraying Jesus had a profound impact on the perception of loyalty and integrity in Jewish culture.
16.interpretation: This verse illustrates Judas's willingness to betray Jesus, highlighting the struggle between good and evil. It sheds light on human fragility in the face of temptation and how seemingly insignificant choices can have eternal consequences.
16.commentaire: Matthew 26:16 reminds us of the importance of our faithfulness to Christ, even when faced with occasions that could lead us astray. Reflecting on Judas's betrayal, we are called to examine our own hearts and motivations, in order to remain steadfast in our commitment to follow Jesus. Let us be vigilant and pray not to yield to the occasions that could distance us from our faith.

mots.sens: The word 'Pascha' refers to the Jewish Passover, which commemorates the liberation of the Israelites from slavery in Egypt. This term has Hebrew roots and evokes the idea of passage and redemption. In the Christian context, it prefigures the sacrifice of Christ, the Lamb of God, who brings true liberation from sin.

The word 'artos' means 'bread' and represents not only physical food but also the spiritual bread, which is Christ himself. In the context of Passover, unleavened bread symbolizes purity and the absence of sin, which is essential for understanding the sacrifice of Jesus. This word underscores the importance of communion with God through Christ.

The term 'symposion' refers to a banquet or shared meal, often associated with moments of fellowship and celebration. In the context of Passover, it emphasizes the importance of communion between the disciples and Jesus, as well as the spiritual significance of sharing a sacred meal. It also foreshadows Christian communion in the New Testament.

17.epoque: This passage is set in the 1st century, during the time of the Jewish Passover, a key moment for the Jewish people, marked by deep religious rituals and traditions.
17.passage: In this chapter, Jesus prepares for his arrest and crucifixion. The disciples' request to prepare for Passover shows their desire to follow Jewish customs while being in communion with their master.
17.culture: Passover is one of the most important festivals in Jewish culture, symbolizing deliverance and collective memory. Ritual meals are moments of family and spiritual gathering.
17.interpretation: This verse highlights the importance of spiritual preparation to meet Christ. The disciples' question reveals their desire to understand and actively participate in the work of Jesus, who is about to accomplish his redemptive mission.
17.commentaire: This passage calls us to be attentive to how we prepare our hearts to meet the Lord. Like the disciples, we must seek to be in communion with Christ, recognizing the depth of his sacrifice. The preparation for Passover invites us to reflect on our own spiritual lives and to engage in an authentic relationship with God.

mots.sens: This term designates a 'ruler' or 'chief', often used to describe civil or religious authorities. In the biblical context, it can also refer to figures of authority who have a role in spiritual or social leadership. Theologically, this reminds us that Jesus, as Master, has authority over all things, including the events leading up to his crucifixion.

This word means 'Passover' and refers to the Jewish festival that commemorates the liberation of the Israelites from slavery in Egypt. Passover is a powerful symbol of redemption and sacrifice, prefiguring the ultimate sacrifice of Christ. In this verse, the mention of Passover underscores the importance of Jesus's sacrifice, who is the Lamb of God, and his role in fulfilling God's promises.

This term means 'disciple' or 'student', and refers to those who follow a master to learn from him. In the New Testament, it is often used to refer to the apostles of Jesus. Spiritually, this evokes the idea of commitment and the intimate relationship between the disciple and the Master, emphasizing the call to discipleship in the Christian life.

18.epoque: This passage is set in the context of 1st century Palestine, under Roman occupation, where religious and political tensions were high.
18.passage: In this chapter, Jesus prepares for his imminent crucifixion, and he establishes the final moments with his disciples. This verse announces the celebration of Passover, a central event in Jewish tradition, marking a decisive moment in God's redemptive plan.
18.culture: Passover was an essential Jewish festival, symbolizing liberation and the collective memory of the people of Israel. It involved precise rituals, such as the sacrifice of a lamb, which echoes in the sacrifice of Jesus.
18.interpretation: This verse reveals Jesus's sovereignty over the unfolding events, indicating that his sacrifice is planned and necessary. It also shows the importance of the community of disciples in the divine plan, emphasizing that Passover is a moment of communion and spiritual revelation.
18.commentaire: This passage reminds us that Jesus is aware of his destiny and chooses to share this crucial moment with his disciples. As Christians, we are called to recognize the significance of Passover and to live in communion with Christ, celebrating his sacrifice and committing to follow him faithfully. This invites us to reflect on our own relationship with the Master and our role as disciples in today's world.

mots.sens: This verb means 'to order' or 'to command'. It is used to indicate an instruction given with authority. In the context of this verse, it emphasizes Jesus' position as a master and spiritual guide, whose directives are followed by his disciples. This highlights the importance of obedience to the word of Christ in the believer's life.

The term 'Passover' refers to the Jewish feast celebrating the liberation of the Israelites from slavery in Egypt. It is laden with theological meanings, symbolizing redemption and sacrifice. In the New Testament, Passover takes on an additional dimension with the sacrifice of Jesus, the true Lamb of God, who offers redemption to humanity.

This word means 'disciple' or 'student'. It designates those who follow a teacher, learning from him and committing to live according to his teachings. In this verse, it underscores the commitment of the disciples to Jesus, illustrating the call to discipleship in the Christian life, where obedience and the application of Christ's teachings are essential.

19.epoque: This verse is set in the context of the first century, at a time when Judaism and religious practices were deeply rooted in Israelite culture, and when Passover was a central celebration of Jewish identity.
19.passage: This passage is part of the account of the Last Supper, where Jesus prepares his disciples for the imminent crucifixion. It underscores the importance of Passover, which foreshadows Christ's sacrifice for the salvation of humanity.
19.culture: Passover was a time for family and community gathering, where rites and traditions were observed carefully. This reflects the importance of collective memory and the transmission of beliefs through generations.
19.interpretation: The obedience of the disciples to Jesus' command demonstrates their devotion and trust in him. It reminds us that following Christ involves responding to his instructions with diligence and faith, recognizing his authority in our lives.
19.commentaire: This verse teaches us the importance of obedience to the word of God. By preparing for Passover according to Jesus' instructions, the disciples illustrate a model of active faith, where listening and action go hand in hand. As believers, we are called to live in the same way, putting into practice Christ's teachings in our daily lives.

mots.sens: This word designates Jesus, the Savior and the Christ. His name means 'Yahweh saves', highlighting his divine role in the salvation of humanity. In this verse, Jesus' presence at the table with his disciples marks the beginning of the institution of the Lord's Supper, thus revealing his intention to seal a new covenant through his sacrifice.

This term means 'disciples' and refers to the twelve men chosen by Jesus to follow him and learn from him. The word evokes a relationship of teaching and learning, as well as a deep commitment to Jesus' mission. Their presence at the table underscores the importance of the community of believers in the Christian faith.

This word means 'table' and symbolizes both a place of communion and sharing. In the Jewish context, the table is a sacred space where communal meals take place, strengthening the bonds between participants. In this verse, the table becomes the place of the establishment of the new covenant, where Jesus shares his body and blood with his disciples.

This word means 'evening' and indicates the time of day when this crucial event takes place. Evening is often associated with moments of reflection and family gathering in Jewish culture. In the context of this passage, evening marks the beginning of Christ's Passion, a moment of transition to the ultimate sacrifice.

20.epoque: This passage is set in the 1st century, at a time when the Jewish people lived under Roman occupation, with strong messianic expectations. Jesus' disciples were in full anticipation of the events that would unfold during the Jewish Passover.
20.passage: In Matthew 26, the chapter focuses on the last moments of Jesus before his crucifixion. This verse introduces the Passover meal, a key moment where Jesus reveals the depth of his love and sacrifice for his disciples.
20.culture: The evening meal, especially during Passover, is of great importance in Jewish culture, symbolizing liberation and communion. It is a time of sharing and memory, where families gather to celebrate together the works of God.
20.interpretation: The fact that Jesus sits at the table with the twelve disciples symbolizes the intimacy and communion he desires to establish with them. This moment also foreshadows the institution of the Lord's Supper, an act that transcends time and is at the heart of the Christian faith, reminding believers of Christ's sacrifice.
20.commentaire: This verse reminds us of the importance of communion with Christ and among believers. By sharing this meal, Jesus invites us to participate in his grace and love. As today's disciples, we are called to gather around him, to celebrate his presence, and to live in community, supporting one another in our walk of faith.

mots.sens: This verb means 'to deliver', 'to betray', or 'to hand over'. It is composed of 'para' (beside) and 'dídōmi' (to give), thus indicating the idea of giving someone to a third party, often in a context of betrayal. In this verse, it underscores the gravity of Judas' act, who, although a disciple, chooses to betray his Master. Spiritually, this evokes the struggle between fidelity and betrayal, a central theme in the relationship between man and God.

This term means 'truth' and is derived from the root 'a-' (negation) and 'lethe' (forgetfulness), which implies a revelation of what is real and authentic. In the context of this verse, Jesus affirms a profound truth about human nature and betrayal, thus revealing the shadow that weighs even on those who follow him. Theologically, this reminds us that the truth of our hearts is often exposed in moments of crisis.

This word means 'one' and emphasizes the individuality and uniqueness of the act of betrayal that is about to occur. In this context, Jesus indicates that only one among the twelve disciples will choose to deliver him, which accentuates the gravity of the act and Judas' personal responsibility. This reminds us that even in a group, each individual has a choice to make that can have eternal consequences.

21.epoque: This passage is set in the 1st century, in the context of Palestine under Roman rule, where political and religious tensions were high.
21.passage: This verse is part of the account of the Last Supper, where Jesus shares a final meal with his disciples before his crucifixion, a moment filled with emotion and revelation.
21.culture: In the Jewish culture of the time, a shared meal held great importance, symbolizing communion and covenant. Judas' betrayal in this context underscores the tragic irony of his decision.
21.interpretation: By announcing that one of his disciples will betray him, Jesus highlights the reality of human weakness and the struggle against sin, even among those who follow him closely. This challenges us regarding our own fidelity and commitment to Christ.
21.commentaire: This verse reminds us that betrayal can come from those who are close to us, but it also calls us to examine our own hearts. Are we faithful to our commitment to Christ, or are we tempted to betray him through our actions or choices? The truth revealed by Jesus should lead us to introspection and a life of authentic devotion.

mots.sens: This term refers to a group of people sharing a common culture, language, or nationality. In the biblical context, it can refer to nations or peoples, but also to the idea of unity and belonging. Spiritually, this emphasizes the importance of the community of believers and the collective responsibility towards God.

This word means 'Lord' and is used to denote supreme authority. In the New Testament, it is often employed to speak of Jesus Christ, thus affirming His divinity and role as Savior. The use of this term here underscores the disciples' recognition of Jesus' authority, as well as their submission to Him.

This word means 'sorrowful' or 'sad', and it expresses deep emotional pain. In this verse, it describes the disciples' state of mind in light of the revelation of betrayal among them. This highlights the seriousness of the situation and the emotional impact that sin and betrayal can have on the community of believers.

22.epoque: This passage is set in the context of the last week of Jesus on earth, just before His crucifixion, a moment of tension and revelation for His disciples.
22.passage: In Matthew 26, Jesus announces that one of His disciples will betray Him, causing deep sorrow among them. This moment is crucial as it reveals not only the human nature of the disciples but also Jesus' foresight regarding His passion.
22.culture: At that time, betrayal was considered one of the worst acts of infidelity, especially in the context of a relationship as intimate as that between Jesus and His disciples. This culture of loyalty makes the question 'Is it I, Lord?' even more poignant.
22.interpretation: The question posed by each disciple shows an awareness of their own weakness and potential to sin. This underscores the necessity of constant vigilance and humility before God, recognizing that each of us can fall into betrayal or sin.
22.commentaire: This verse reminds us of the importance of self-examination and confession in our walk with Christ. By questioning our faithfulness, we are invited to stay close to our Lord and seek His grace to avoid betraying Him. It also encourages us to pray for our brothers and sisters, that they may remain steadfast in faith.

mots.sens: This term means 'tradition' or 'delivery'. In the context of Matthew 26:23, it evokes the notion of betrayal and handing someone over to their enemies. The root of the word refers to the idea of transmitting something precious, but here, it highlights the gravity of Judas' betrayal, who delivers Jesus despite their closeness. Spiritually, this reminds us of the fragility of human relationships and the need for vigilance in our commitment to Christ.

This personal pronoun means 'you' and emphasizes proximity and intimacy. In this verse, it is used to refer to Judas, highlighting the betrayal of one who shared a meal with Jesus. This illustrates the depth of betrayal, as Judas is not a stranger, but a companion. Theologically, this challenges us regarding human nature and the capacity to betray even those we love.

This word means 'communion' or 'partnership'. In the context of this passage, it evokes the idea of sharing and intimate connection between Jesus and His disciples. Communion is a central theme in Christian life, and here it is tragically contrasted with betrayal. This reminds us that our communion with Christ must be protected and valued, as it is essential to our faith.

23.epoque: This passage is set in the 1st century, during a time of heightened religious and political tensions in Palestine, with Roman occupation and tensions between Jewish religious authorities and messianic movements.
23.passage: Matthew 26 describes the events leading up to the crucifixion of Jesus. This verse is part of the account of the Last Supper, where Jesus announces Judas' betrayal, highlighting the drama unfolding in the heart of one of His disciples.
23.culture: In Jewish culture, sharing a meal was an act of communion and friendship. The betrayal of a friend during such an act was particularly shocking and revealing of the depth of disloyalty.
23.interpretation: Jesus reveals here that the betrayal comes from one who shares His meal, emphasizing the pain of betrayal within the community of disciples. This reminds us that even in the closest circles, loyalty can be tested. Spiritually, this challenges us to be vigilant in our relationships and not to take our communion with Christ for granted.
23.commentaire: This verse teaches us the importance of faithfulness in our relationships, both with God and with others. Judas' betrayal warns us against the dangers of hypocrisy and spiritual indifference. As disciples of Christ, we must cultivate an authentic relationship with Him, ensuring that our hearts remain faithful and engaged, even in the face of temptations.

mots.sens: This expression literally means 'Son of Man'. It is used in Scripture to refer to Jesus, highlighting His humanity and messianic role. In this verse, it evokes Jesus' divine mission and destiny, while also shedding light on His identification with humanity. This also underscores the gravity of the ensuing betrayal, as the Son of Man is destined to fulfill the Scriptures.

This verb means 'to deliver' or 'to betray'. It implies handing someone over to another, often in a context of betrayal. In the verse, it refers to Judas, who delivers Jesus, highlighting the horror of this act. Spiritually, this evokes the question of free will and the tragic consequences of betrayal.

This term means 'cursed' or 'unfortunate'. It expresses deep desolation and separation from God. In the context of this verse, it underscores the severity of Judas' sin, suggesting that his betrayal places him under severe judgment. This reminds believers of the seriousness of our choices and their eternal consequences.

24.epoque: This passage is set in the context of 1st century Palestine, under Roman occupation, where religious and political tensions were high.
24.passage: Matthew 26 describes the final days of Jesus before His crucifixion, highlighting Judas' betrayal and Jesus' anguish in the Garden of Gethsemane.
24.culture: In Jewish culture, betrayal was considered one of the worst sins, and delivering an innocent person to death had profound moral and spiritual implications.
24.interpretation: This verse highlights the fatality of Jesus' destiny, while also emphasizing Judas' heavy responsibility. The statement 'it would be better for him if he had not been born' reveals the gravity of the betrayal and the eternal consequences that follow.
24.commentaire: This passage reminds us of the importance of our choices and our faithfulness to Christ. Judas' betrayal serves as a warning about the dangers of drifting away from God. As believers, we are called to remain steadfast in our faith and not allow temptations to divert us from our divine mission.

mots.sens: The name 'Ioudas' is derived from the Hebrew 'Yehouda', which means 'wolf' or 'praise the Lord'. In the context of the New Testament, Judas is often associated with betrayal and disappointment, thus representing the choice to turn away from the truth. The theological significance of this name reminds us that even those who are close to Jesus can stray from the faith, highlighting the importance of spiritual vigilance.

This verb means 'to deliver', 'to betray', or 'to hand over'. It evokes the act of betrayal that Judas commits by delivering Jesus to the authorities. Spiritually, this word underscores the gravity of betrayal, not only against a friend but also against the Son of God, and highlights the sacrifice that Jesus is about to make for humanity.

The term 'rabbí' means 'my master' or 'teacher', and is a title of respect used to refer to a Jewish teacher. In this verse, Judas addresses Jesus with this title, which underscores the irony of his betrayal. It also reveals the complex relationship between Judas and Jesus, where Judas acknowledges Jesus' authority while choosing to betray him.

25.epoque: The passage is set in the 1st century, in a context where religious and political tensions were high in Judea, with a strong Roman presence and messianic expectations among the Jewish people.
25.passage: This verse is found in the account of the Last Supper, where Jesus shares one last meal with his disciples before his crucifixion, thus establishing a crucial moment in the history of salvation.
25.culture: In the Jewish culture of the time, a shared meal had a profound significance, symbolizing intimacy and communion. Judas' betrayal during this sacred moment accentuates the gravity of his act.
25.interpretation: Judas, by asking 'Is it I, Rabbi?', shows an attempt at concealment and denial, even as he is about to commit an unforgivable act. Jesus' response, 'You have said so', not only confirms the imminent betrayal but also highlights Jesus' perfect knowledge of human hearts.
25.commentaire: This verse reminds us that proximity to Jesus does not guarantee faithfulness to him. It is essential to examine ourselves and to be vigilant in our relationship with Christ, so as not to fall into betrayal through conscious or unconscious choices. Judas' question challenges us: are we truly committed to following Jesus, or are we flirting with betrayal through our actions and daily choices?

mots.sens: The word 'ἄρτος' refers to bread, a staple food in Jewish culture. It symbolizes sustenance and life, and is often associated with communion with God. In the context of this verse, it represents the body of Christ, emphasizing the idea that Jesus gives himself to spiritually nourish his disciples.

The term 'εὐχαριστέω' means 'to give thanks' or 'to be grateful'. It is derived from 'εὐχαριστία', which evokes gratitude towards God. In this passage, the act of giving thanks before breaking the bread underscores the importance of recognition in the relationship with God and prepares the hearts of the disciples to receive the gift of Christ.

The word 'σῶμα' means 'body'. In the context of this verse, it refers to the physical body of Jesus, which will be sacrificed for the salvation of humanity. It also evokes the notion of the unity of the body of Christ, the Church, and the communion among believers, reinforcing the idea that Jesus' sacrifice is central to the Christian faith.

26.epoque: This passage takes place during the first century, at the time of the Jewish Passover, a feast that commemorates Israel's liberation from slavery in Egypt.
26.passage: Chapter 26 of Matthew describes the events leading up to the crucifixion of Jesus, including the Last Supper with his disciples, where he institutes the Lord's Supper.
26.culture: In Jewish culture, bread is a symbol of life and communion. A shared meal is an act of unity and solidarity, strengthening the bonds among participants.
26.interpretation: Jesus, by taking the bread and declaring 'This is my body', announces the imminent sacrifice he will make for humanity. This gesture establishes a new covenant, where the bread becomes a symbol of his presence and sacrifice for salvation.
26.commentaire: This verse reminds us of the importance of gratitude in our relationship with God, inviting us to recognize Christ's sacrifice. By partaking in the Lord's Supper, we are called to remember his broken body for us and to live in communion with one another as members of the body of Christ.

mots.sens: This word means 'cup' and refers to a vessel used for drinking. In the context of the Jewish Passover, it symbolizes the blood of the Passover lamb, which was sacrificed for redemption. Spiritually, it evokes the sacrifice of Christ, whose blood is shed for the forgiveness of sins, establishing a new covenant between God and humanity.

This term means 'having given thanks' and comes from the root 'eucharistia', which denotes the act of thanksgiving. In this verse, it emphasizes the importance of gratitude towards God before sharing the cup, reminding us that every act of communion must be rooted in recognition of divine goodness. It teaches us that gratitude is essential in our relationship with God.

27.epoque: This passage is set in the 1st century, during the Jewish Passover, a central feast for the Jewish people, marking the liberation from Egypt and God's promise to his people.
27.passage: In chapter 26 of Matthew, Jesus celebrates the Last Supper with his disciples, a crucial moment before his crucifixion. This passage highlights the institution of the Lord's Supper, a symbolic act of communion and sacrifice.
27.culture: In Jewish culture, sharing wine and bread during sacred meals is an act of communion and remembrance. It reinforces the idea of community and spiritual connection among participants.
27.interpretation: Jesus' invitation to 'drink from it, all of you' emphasizes the universality of his sacrifice. It reminds us that salvation is offered to all, without exception, and that we are called to actively participate in this new covenant through faith.
27.commentaire: This verse teaches us the importance of communion in our Christian life. By drinking from the cup, we affirm our participation in Christ's sacrifice and our commitment to him. It is a call to live in gratitude and to share this grace with others, bearing witness to God's love in our daily lives.

mots.sens: This term means 'blood' and is often associated with life, purification, and atonement in the Bible. In the context of the covenant, blood represents the necessary sacrifice to establish a relationship between God and humanity. Theologically, the blood of Christ is essential for the remission of sins, as it embodies the ultimate gift of life for the salvation of believers.

This word translates to 'covenant' and refers to a solemn agreement between two parties. In the biblical context, it evokes God's promise to His people, often sealed by blood. The new covenant, inaugurated by the sacrifice of Christ, offers a renewed and intimate relationship with God, marked by grace and redemption.

This term means 'remission' or 'forgiveness' and implies the release from debts or sins. In the New Testament, it emphasizes the divine grace that erases the faults of believers. Spiritually, the remission of sins through the blood of Christ is the foundation of reconciliation between God and man, offering a new life in Christ.

28.epoque: This passage is set in the context of the first century, during a time when Judaism was deeply rooted in traditions and ritual sacrifices. Jewish believers were awaiting the coming of the Messiah, who would bring redemption and the fulfillment of God's promises.
28.passage: Matthew 26:28 is found in the account of the Last Supper, where Jesus institutes the Lord's Supper. This moment is crucial as it marks the transition between the old and the new covenant, highlighting the importance of Christ's sacrifice for the salvation of sinners.
28.culture: In Jewish culture, blood had a sacred significance, often associated with sacrifices in the temple for the atonement of sins. The idea of the covenant was also central, reminding of God's promises to His people, which made Jesus' teaching even more impactful for His disciples.
28.interpretation: This verse reveals that the blood of Jesus is the foundation of the new covenant, sealing the forgiveness of sins for all who believe. It emphasizes the universality of the offer of salvation, 'for many,' indicating that redemption is accessible to all who accept Christ's sacrifice.
28.commentaire: Matthew 26:28 reminds us of the importance of Jesus' sacrifice for our redemption. By participating in communion, we celebrate not only the forgiveness of our sins but also our commitment to the new covenant with God. This calls us to live in gratitude and obedience, recognizing the price paid for our salvation.

mots.sens: This word refers to wine, produced from the fermentation of grapes. In the biblical context, it often symbolizes joy, abundance, and communion. Spiritually, wine is also associated with the covenant between God and His people, and here, it foreshadows the sacrifice of Christ and the new covenant established by His blood.

This term means 'kingdom' and evokes the royal reign of God. It denotes not only a place but also a spiritual reality where God's sovereignty is exercised. In this verse, it underscores the eschatological hope of believers, who await the fullness of communion with Christ in the eternal kingdom.

This word means 'father' and expresses an intimate and protective relationship. In the context of the Christian faith, it emphasizes God's fatherhood and His desire for relationship with humanity. Here, it highlights the promise of future communion with the Heavenly Father, reinforcing the idea of a spiritual family.

29.epoque: This verse is set in the context of the first century, during a time when Judaism and Christianity were emerging in a Roman environment. The practices of the Jewish Passover are essential, marking a transition to the new covenant in Christ.
29.passage: Matthew 26 describes the events of the Last Supper, where Jesus institutes the Lord's Supper. This moment is crucial as it announces Judas' betrayal and the imminent sacrifice of Jesus, while establishing a new relationship between God and humanity.
29.culture: In Jewish culture, wine is a central element of festive rituals and celebrations. It symbolizes joy and covenant, and its use during Passover underscores the importance of communion and remembrance of God's acts toward His people.
29.interpretation: This verse highlights Jesus' anticipation for the coming kingdom, where He will share wine again with His disciples. It evokes a promise of restoration and eternal communion, reinforcing the Christian hope in life after death and the fullness of God's presence.
29.commentaire: This passage reminds us of the importance of communion with Christ, both in the present and in the future. As we await Jesus' return, we are called to live in communion with one another, to celebrate our faith, and to anticipate the joy of eternal life in the kingdom of God. May this encourage us to remain faithful and to share this hope with those around us.

mots.sens: This verb means 'to sing' and is often used in the context of praise and worship. In Jewish tradition, singing was an essential expression of faith, especially during religious celebrations. Spiritually, singing hymns before going to the Mount of Olives underscores the importance of praise in moments of transition and spiritual preparation.

This term refers to a 'hymn' or 'song' that is often associated with hymns of praise or psalms. Hymns are expressions of faith and communion with God, serving to strengthen both the community and the individual in their relationship with the divine. In the context of this verse, the hymns sung by Jesus and His disciples reveal their commitment to God, even in the face of imminent adversity.

This word means 'mountain' and often evokes places of encounter with God in the Bible. Mountains are symbols of stability and proximity to the divine, where significant revelations have occurred. In this passage, the Mount of Olives becomes the setting for intense prayer and spiritual struggle, highlighting the importance of such places in the life of faith.

30.epoque: This passage is set in the context of the first century, during the time of the Jewish Passover, a crucial moment for Jews commemorating the liberation from Egypt.
30.passage: This verse is found at the end of Jesus' last meal with His disciples, just before His arrest. It marks a transition to the suffering and passion of Christ, while emphasizing the importance of praise even in difficult moments.
30.culture: In Jewish culture, singing hymns was a common practice during festive meals and religious celebrations, reinforcing community and spiritual identity.
30.interpretation: This verse reminds us that praise should precede our trials. Jesus, by singing hymns, shows us that even in times of great distress, we must keep our hearts turned toward God and express our faith through praise.
30.commentaire: This passage encourages us to integrate praise into our daily lives, especially when facing challenges. Like Jesus, we must remember that singing hymns can strengthen our faith and prepare us to face trials. By cultivating an attitude of praise, we open our hearts to God's peace and presence in our lives.

mots.sens: The word 'ποιμήν' refers to a shepherd, one who cares for the sheep. In the biblical context, it evokes the protective and nurturing relationship between the shepherd and his flock, often symbolizing spiritual leadership. Jesus presents himself here as the shepherd who, when struck, causes the scattering of his sheep, highlighting the fragility of his disciples in the face of adversity and the importance of their dependence on him.

The term 'σκορπίζω' means to scatter or disperse. It evokes not only the physical separation of the sheep but also the loss of communion and spiritual security. In this verse, it foreshadows the crisis that the disciples will face after Jesus' arrest, emphasizing their vulnerability and the need to remain united around their Master.

The word 'πρόβατα' refers to sheep, symbolizing the believers or disciples of Christ. Sheep are often used in the Bible to represent those who follow the shepherd, Jesus. In this passage, their scattering after the blow struck at the shepherd underscores the necessity of divine guidance and the fragility of human faith in the face of trials.

The verb 'σκανδαλίζω' means to cause to stumble or to be an occasion for scandal. It implies a testing of faith, where the disciples will be confronted with situations that could cause them to waver. Jesus announces here that he will be the cause of this trial, thus revealing the depth of his sacrifice and the necessity of faith in times of crisis.

31.epoque: This passage is set in the context of the last week of Jesus' life, just before his crucifixion, a period marked by increasing tensions between Jesus and the Jewish religious authorities.
31.passage: In Matthew 26, Jesus prepares his disciples for his imminent arrest. This verse highlights the prophecy of Zechariah 13:7, which announces that the shepherd will be struck, leading to the scattering of the sheep, which is a foreshadowing of the disciples' abandonment during the crucifixion.
31.culture: At that time, the role of the shepherd was crucial in Jewish society, representing protection and care. The metaphor of the shepherd and the sheep is commonly used in the Old Testament to illustrate the relationship between God and his people.
31.interpretation: Jesus, as the shepherd, identifies with the prophecy and announces that his suffering will lead to a crisis for his disciples. This scattering of the sheep symbolizes not only their physical abandonment but also the necessity of their faith in difficult moments, emphasizing the importance of remaining attached to Christ even in trials.
31.commentaire: This verse reminds us that even the closest to Jesus can falter in times of crisis. It calls us to recognize our dependence on Christ, our shepherd, and to seek strength in him when we face trials. By understanding that our faith can be tested, we are encouraged to anchor ourselves more deeply in the Word of God and to remain united as a community of believers.

mots.sens: This word means 'to rise' or 'to resurrect.' It is derived from the root 'ἀνά' (ana), which means 'up,' and 'ἵστημι' (histēmi), which means 'to stand.' In the context of this verse, it evokes the power of Jesus' resurrection, which is not just a return to life, but a victory over death and sin, thus bringing the hope of eternal life to all believers.

This term means 'to precede' or 'to go before.' It is composed of 'προ' (pro), which means 'before,' and 'ἄγω' (agō), which means 'to lead' or 'to guide.' 32.epoque: This passage is set in the context of the last week of Jesus' earthly life, just before his crucifixion, in an environment marked by anxiety and uncertainty among his disciples.

32.culture: Galilee was perceived as a marginal region, often looked down upon by the elites of Jerusalem. However, it is there that Jesus chose to begin his ministry, showing that the kingdom of God extends beyond established social and religious boundaries.
32.interpretation: This verse reminds us that the resurrection of Jesus is central to our faith. It is not just a historical event but a living promise that calls us to follow him and to live in the hope of our own resurrection.
32.commentaire: Jesus' promise to go before his disciples in Galilee after his resurrection is a source of encouragement for us today. It reminds us that even in our moments of doubt and despair, Jesus is always at work, guiding us toward light and truth. As believers, we are called to live in this hope and to share the good news of his resurrection with those around us.

mots.sens: This word means 'to cause to fall' or 'to be an occasion for stumbling.' It is derived from 'skandalon,' which refers to a trap or stumbling block. Peter, asserting that he will never be an occasion for stumbling, expresses his determination to remain faithful, but he is unaware of his own weakness.

In the context of Peter's declaration, it reinforces his commitment to Jesus, showing a self-confidence that can lead to spiritual pride. This reminds us of the importance of humility and vigilance in our walk with Christ.

This word means 'other' or 'different.' In this verse, it refers to the other disciples, highlighting that Peter sees himself as distinct from the others. This brings to light the danger of comparison and presumption in our faith, as each is called to a personal relationship with God, without considering oneself superior to others.

33.epoque: This passage is set in the context of Jesus' ministry, shortly before his crucifixion, at a time when tensions between Jesus and the religious authorities were at their peak.
33.passage: In Matthew 26, Jesus tells his disciples that they will all forsake him. Peter, confidently, declares that he will never be an occasion for stumbling, illustrating his passion but also his blindness to his own weakness.
33.culture: At that time, loyalty and honor were paramount values in Jewish culture. The disciples, as companions of Jesus, felt strong social pressure to remain faithful, but this could also lead to attitudes of pride.
33.interpretation: Peter's assertion reveals an excessive self-confidence, often present in those who believe they have unwavering faith. Spiritually, this teaches us that true strength lies in our dependence on God and not in our own assurance.
33.commentaire: This verse reminds us of the importance of humility in our Christian walk. Like Peter, we may be tempted to think we are above potential falls, but it is crucial to remain vigilant and seek strength in Christ. Recognizing our weakness drives us to depend on God's grace, which is always sufficient to support us in trials.

mots.sens: This verb means 'to deny' or 'to renounce'. In the context of this verse, it evokes the idea of publicly renouncing an affiliation or belief, specifically Peter's relationship with Jesus. The root of this word implies a breach of trust and a abandonment of loyalty, which underscores the seriousness of the act of denying Christ. Spiritually, this reminds us of human fragility in the face of fear and pressure, even for those who are close to Jesus.
